text: On the dates indicated in the appended table, the applicants participated in political demonstrations.
The applicants were arrested at the venue of the political demonstrations.
The applicants were subsequently convicted of an administrative offence.
The applicants' details are set out in the appended table.
The Government were represented by Mr G. Matyushkin, Representative of the Russian Federation at the European Court of Human Rights.
The Government were subsequently represented by Mr A. Fedorov, Head of the Office of the Representative of the Russian Federation at the European Court of Human Rights.
The Government were subsequently represented by Mr M. Galperin, Representative of the Russian Federation at the European Court of Human Rights.
The facts of the case, as submitted by the parties, may be summarised as follows.
On the dates indicated in the appended table, the applicants participated in political demonstrations.
The applicants were apprehended at the venue of the political demonstrations.
The applicants were transferred to police stations in Moscow after being apprehended.
Relevant administrative records were drawn up at the police stations in Moscow.
The administrative offence records were based on the reports and explanations of the police officers who had arrested the applicants.
The first applicant, Mr Akhunov, was released several hours after being apprehended.
The second applicant, Mr Nemuchinskiy, remained in detention until the court hearing the next day.
On the dates stipulated in the appended table, the applicants were convicted under the Code of Administrative Offences.
The first applicant, Mr Akhunov, was convicted under Article 20.2 § 5 of the Code of Administrative Offences, which concerns violating the established procedure for the conduct of a public assembly.
The first applicant, Mr Akhunov, was ordered to pay a fine of 10,000 Russian roubles.
The second applicant, Mr Nemuchinskiy, was convicted under Article 19.3 § 1 of the Code of Administrative Offences, which concerns refusal to obey the lawful order of a police officer.
The second applicant, Mr Nemuchinskiy, was sentenced to administrative imprisonment of fifteen days.
The domestic courts relied on the administrative records and the reports and explanations of the police officers when convicting the applicants.
The domestic courts considered it unlawful that the applicants had shouted slogans during the demonstrations.
The domestic courts considered it unlawful that the applicants had participated in a public assembly in respect of which no advance notification had been submitted to the authorities.
A summary of the relevant domestic law can be found in Navalnyy v. Russia [GC] (nos. 29580/12 and 4 others, §§ 46-47, 15 November 2018).
The domestic legal provisions governing administrative transfer (escorting) and detention are set out in the case of Butkevich v. Russia (no. 5865/07, §§ 33-36, 13 February 2018).

According to Article 31.9 of the Code of Administrative Offences, if a decision imposing an administrative punishment is not enforced within two years from its entry into force, it can no longer be executed.

According to Article 31.9 of the Code of Administrative Offences, the time when enforcement of a decision imposing an administrative punishment is suspended or stayed is excluded from the two-year enforcement period.
